slides.content: Extraction steps: 1. Concentration of ore. 2. Production of metal (reduction). 3. Purification. Most active metals (K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al) are extracted by electrolysis. Less active metals (Fe, Zn) are extracted by chemical reduction. Noble metals are found free.
slides.notes: Metallurgy: science of extracting metals and making alloys.

slides.title: Aluminium: Extraction and Properties
slides.content: Extraction: Hall-Héroult process. Bauxite (Al₂O₃·2H₂O) → purify to Al₂O₃ → dissolve in molten cryolite → electrolyze. Cathode: 4Al³⁺ + 12e⁻ → 4Al. Anode: 6O²⁻ + 3C → 3CO₂ + 12e⁻. Properties: lightweight, good conductor, corrosion-resistant (oxide layer). Uses: aircraft, cookware, packaging, power lines.
slides.notes: Cryolite (Na₃AlF₆) lowers melting point of Al₂O₃ from 2045°C to 1000°C.

slides.title: Iron: Extraction and Properties
slides.content: Extraction: Blast furnace. Iron ore (Fe₂O₃), coke, limestone. Reactions: Coke + O₂ → CO₂. CO₂ + C → 2CO. Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. Limestone: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. CaO + SiO₂ → CaSiO₃ (slag). Pig iron (impure, 3.5-4.5% C) → refined to steel (Bessemer converter, open-hearth, basic oxygen process). Wrought iron (purest). Properties: reactive, rusts in moist air, reacts with acids to produce H₂.
slides.notes: Steel: alloy of iron with controlled carbon content. Alloy steels: contain other metals (Cr, Ni) for specific properties.

slides.title: Copper: Extraction and Properties
slides.content: Extraction: from chalcopyrite (CuFeS₂). Roasting: 2CuFeS₂ + 4O₂ → Cu₂S + 2FeO + 3SO₂. Smelting: Cu₂S + O₂ → 2Cu + SO₂ (blister copper, 98.5-99.5% pure). Refining: Electrolytic refining (impure Cu anode, pure Cu cathode, CuSO₄ electrolyte). Cathode: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. Anode: Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻. Properties: good conductor, malleable, ductile. Uses: electrical wires, alloys (brass, bronze).
slides.notes: Copper does not react with dilute acids but reacts with oxidizing acids (HNO₃, hot H₂SO₄).

slides.title: Properties of Nonmetals
slides.content: Nonmetals: non-lustrous, non-malleable, non-ductile, poor conductors, low density, non-sonorous. Chemical: gain electrons (oxidizing agents), form acidic oxides, do not react with acids (usually).
slides.notes: Examples: N₂ (gas), S (solid), Cl₂ (gas).

slides.title: Nitrogen and Phosphorus
slides.content: Nitrogen: from fractional distillation of liquid air. Inert due to triple bond. Reacts with metals (nitrides), O₂ (NO, NO₂), H₂ (NH₃, Haber process). Uses: fertilizer, refrigerant. Phosphorus: from phosphate rock (Ca₃(PO₄)₂), silica, coke in electric furnace. Allotropes: white (reactive, stored under water), red (stable). Forms P₄O₆, P₄O₁₀ (acidic oxides). Uses: matches, fertilizers.
slides.notes: Haber process: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ (Fe catalyst, 400-600°C, 200-300 atm).

slides.title: Oxygen, Sulfur, and Chlorine
slides.content: Oxygen: from fractional distillation of liquid air. Supports combustion, reacts with metals (basic oxides) and nonmetals (acidic oxides). Ozone (O₃) allotrope. Sulfur: from underground deposits (Frasch process). Allotropes: rhombic, monoclinic. Reacts with metals (sulphides), O₂ (SO₂, SO₃, Contact process for H₂SO₄). Chlorine: from electrolysis of brine (NaCl). Greenish-yellow, strong oxidizing agent. Reacts with metals (chlorides), H₂ (HCl), displaces Br₂/I₂. Uses: bleach, disinfectant.
slides.notes: Contact process: S + O₂ → SO₂, 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ (V₂O₅ catalyst), SO₃ + H₂SO₄ → H₂S₂O₇, H₂S₂O₇ + H₂O → 2H₂SO₄.

slides.title: Introduction to Organic Chemistry
slides.content: Organic chemistry: study of carbon compounds (except simple ones like CO, CO₂, carbonates). Vitalism: disproved by Wöhler's synthesis of urea (1828). Catenation: carbon's ability to form chains and rings. Functional groups: atoms/bonds with characteristic chemical behavior.
slides.notes: Organic compounds: over 50 million known.

slides.title: Alkanes: Structure and Nomenclature
slides.content: Alkanes: saturated hydrocarbons, CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. IUPAC nomenclature: find longest chain (parent), number to give lowest locants, name substituents (alkyl groups) alphabetically. Alkyl groups: formed by removing H from alkane, named with -yl.
slides.notes: Examples: CH₄ (methane), C₂H₆ (ethane), C₃H₈ (propane).

slides.title: Isomerism in Alkanes
slides.content: Structural isomerism: same formula, different connectivity. Number of isomers increases with carbon atoms. C₄H₁₀: 2 isomers (n-butane, isobutane). C₅H₁₂: 3 isomers. C₆H₁₄: 5 isomers.
slides.notes: Branched alkanes have lower boiling points than straight-chain isomers.

slides.title: Properties and Reactions of Alkanes
slides.content: Physical: nonpolar, insoluble in water, boiling point increases with molecular weight. Chemical: Combustion: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O + heat. Substitution: halogenation (CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl) with light/heat. Cracking: thermal decomposition.
slides.notes: Alkanes are relatively inert (paraffins).

sections.section: 6.3 Unsaturated Hydrocarbons: Alkenes, Alkynes, and Aromatic Hydrocarbons

slides.title: Alkenes (Olefins)
slides.content: Alkenes: CₙH₂ₙ, contain C=C double bond. Nomenclature: -ene suffix, number for double bond. Isomerism: chain, position, and geometrical (cis-trans). Preparation: dehydration of alcohols (H₂SO₄), dehydrohalogenation of alkyl halides (KOH). Reactions: combustion, addition (hydrogenation, halogenation, hydrohalogenation, hydration, polymerization).
slides.notes: Markovnikov's rule: H adds to C with more H's. Br₂/CCl₄ decolorization test for unsaturation.

slides.title: Alkynes
slides.content: Alkynes: CₙH₂ₙ₋₂, contain C≡C triple bond. Simplest: ethyne (acetylene). Reactions: combustion (sooty flame), addition (two-step, e.g., halogenation, hydrogenation). Trimerization of acetylene to benzene.
slides.notes: Uses: oxy-acetylene torch (high temperature flame).

slides.title: Aromatic Hydrocarbons: Benzene
slides.content: Benzene: C₆H₆, resonance-stabilized ring. Does not undergo typical alkene addition reactions. Reactions: combustion, substitution (halogenation, nitration, sulfonation). Nomenclature: monosubstituted (toluene, phenol), disubstituted (ortho, meta, para).
slides.notes: Benzene is carcinogenic. Substitution is characteristic, not addition.

slides.title: Natural Gas and Petroleum
slides.content: Natural gas: mainly methane (CH₄). Petroleum (crude oil): complex mixture of hydrocarbons. Fractional distillation: separates into fractions by boiling point. Fractions: natural gas (C₁-C₄), gasoline (C₅-C₁₀), kerosene (C₁₂-C₁₈), diesel (C₁₅-C₁₈), lubricating oils (>C₁₉), residue. Cracking: breaks large hydrocarbons into smaller ones (e.g., gasoline). Reforming: converts alkanes to aromatics for higher octane rating.
slides.notes: Octane number: measure of anti-knock properties. Isooctane = 100, heptane = 0.

slides.title: Coal
slides.content: Coal: formed from plant matter. Destructive distillation (coking): heating in absence of air produces coal gas, coal tar, and coke. Coal tar is a source of aromatic hydrocarbons (benzene, toluene).
slides.notes: Coke is used as fuel in blast furnaces (iron extraction).
